extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, sociology, and comparative institutions; general readers of social theory
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook/chapter excerpt analyzing the social effects of equality and democratic institutions, listing salient intellectual characteristics of the American people and discussing their causes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire to be abreast of best thought
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. A desire to be abreast of the best thought and work of the world everywhere, to have every form of literature and art adequately represented, and excellent of its kind, so that America shall be felt to hold her own among the nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by the author as the first of the salient intellectual features of the mass of the native population. Presented as an observable tendency rather than a normative prescription. The author later notes that some of these characteristics cannot be wholly attributed to democratic government and may arise from education and a desire for national standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondness for bold and striking effects
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. A fondness for bold and striking effects, a preference for large generalizations and theories which have an air of completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a general taste in the populace; later the author remarks that this preference (and related items) may owe more to general intelligence and education or to national conditions (size, homogeneity) than to democracy per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of refined taste among the multitude
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. An absence among the multitude of refined taste, with a disposition to be attracted rather by brilliance than by delicacy of workmanship; a want of mellowness and inadequate perception of the difference between first-rate work in a quiet style and mere flatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a tendency of the mass, contrasted with the cultivated class; the author warns against attributing this solely to political institutions and suggests causes including size of country and absence of a leisured class dominant in matters of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little respect for canons or traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. Little respect for canons or traditions, accompanied by the notion that new conditions must of necessity produce new ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a characteristic of popular culture; author notes that lack of deference to tradition may accompany democratic habits but is also linked to the social context and national circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undervaluing of special knowledge or experience
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. An undervaluing of special knowledge or experience, except in applied science and in commerce, an idea that an able man can do one thing pretty much as well as another...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighted as a popular attitude toward expertise; the author contrasts admiration for general intelligence with deference to specialized competence and cautions about overattributing this to form of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration for literary or scientific eminence
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. An admiration for literary or scientific eminence, an enthusiasm for anything that can be called genius, with undue eagerness to discover it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded as a positive tendency — admiration for genius — but qualified by the remark that this eagerness can be excessive and interacts with other tendencies (e.g., valuing brilliance over depth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion for novelties
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author later suggests the seventh (and eighth) items "seem due to the general intelligence and education of the people," i.e., this hunger for novelty may stem from broad education and national dynamism rather than democracy alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual impatience and desire for quick results
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. An intellectual impatience, and desire for quick and patent results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linked by the author to general intelligence and education; presented as producing a preference for rapid, demonstrable outcomes rather than slow, nuanced inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-valuing judgments of the multitude
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. An over-valuing of the judgments of the multitude; a disposition to judge by newspaper success work which has not been produced with a view to such success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as a tendency to take popular (newspaper) approval as a standard; the author connects this to democratic self-confidence and warns it can narrow artistic and intellectual ambition by privileging mass approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to mistake bigness for greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. A tendency to mistake bigness for greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a common error in public judgment — conflating scale or visibility with intrinsic quality. The author treats this as one of several interrelated features that shape culture and taste, influenced by national conditions and the public's preferences.
